name: Elena Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kindly Hands Home Care in the market town, and I mostly look after older ladies who want a female carer for washing and dressing. Because I speak two languages, the office sends me the clients who don't have much English, so I'm often the only person they chat to all day. My first call is Mrs Begum at half seven, who insists I eat a paratha before I leave. I like being trusted with people's mothers. What wears me out is the evenings, when I finish at nine and then go round to check on my mother-in-law's sugar levels.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Samir. We married last year, and we rent a flat above the dry cleaner's on the high street. He drives the delivery van for a wholesale bakery, so he's up at four and I'm up at six, and we see each other at dinner if we're lucky. We've got about three weeks of money saved, and we're trying to save for a house before we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. I didn't need AI to change my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the important things in life were never going to come from a computer. Family, faith and good work, that's it. I'd say it at the community centre when the ladies talk about the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means our plans stay slow. Rent goes up, wages don't, and a house deposit feels years away. Samir's bakery lost a big supermarket contract in the summer, so his overtime's down, and that's money we were counting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kindly Hands for the extra Sunday calls, because they pay time and a quarter. I'd keep using the AI on my phone now and then, like I do to translate hospital letters for Mrs Begum's family. And we'd hold off on the new sofa until spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. Not scared, just tired of the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the overtime dropped, what did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month. That's the whole amount we were putting in the house pot. Now we put in maybe fifty, and some months nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for work outside care for better pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. There's the packing plant on the industrial estate, but the hours are worse and you don't help anyone. I'd rather be useful and a bit poorer than pack boxes at the plant on the industrial estate.

I'd say it at the **community centre** when the ladies discuss the news.

do: Ask Kindly Hands for **Sunday calls** at time and a quarter.
Keep using phone AI now and then to **translate hospital letters**.
Hold off on the **new sofa** until spring.
feel: **Heavy**, tired of waiting rather than scared.

fieldNote: Her pressure is **Samir's lost overtime**, which stalled their house savings.

Keep translating clients' hospital letters with the phone AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and planning. That would be the agency office and maybe the bakery's ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should use it if it helps them, but they should train their people, not just throw them out. That's what a good employer does. I'd say it to my manager, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's fine for now. Nobody's built a machine my client Mrs Begum would let wash her. Samir's job is the worry. The bakery's ordering and routes would go to software, and in a few years maybe the vans drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what tools the agency brings in and learn them once the others had. I'd tell Samir to ask his boss about the warehouse supervisor role, because that's people management. And we'd keep the house money going, even if it's only fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For him more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samir say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's fine and stop worrying. Then he'd go quiet for an evening. He's proud, like his dad, he doesn't like being told what to do by his wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coordinator, Hannah, who answers the phones and does the rota. She's a single mum. If a computer does her job, I don't know what she'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years? And robots by 2031? That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should look after each other, as families and communities, and not wait for anyone to save us. I'd say businesses that save money on robots should pay for retraining. I wouldn't want people living on benefits for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think both our jobs are gone by about 2031, Samir's van maybe even sooner. We'd have to forget the house, and probably children for a while. I'd be thirty-one with no trade except care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look into the healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital, since hospitals might keep people longer. I'd cut everything back: no holiday to see my sister, no sofa. And we'd talk to Samir's parents about moving into their spare room to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And a bit sad that our plans would just stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother-in-law about moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be delighted, honestly. She wants us closer anyway, with her sugar. I'd be the one who finds it hard, sharing a kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not to live on benefits. What if there's no other way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd take what we needed, and pay it back by working when we could. But I'd go to family first, then the mosque's help fund, before the government.

I'd say businesses saving on robots should **pay for retraining**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but you could do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to learn something new, and people should get on with it. I'd tell the young ones at the community centre to pick a trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time for one good move. Maybe the nursing associate apprenticeship, because you earn while you learn, and a nurse's work is harder to replace. Samir would need something too, before 2034 when the vans go driverless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the nursing associate apprenticeship next year. I'd use AI now and then for the reading, once I know it's reliable. And Samir would look at an electrician's apprenticeship with his cousin's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel better once we had a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait two years, maybe three, until I'm through the apprenticeship. My mother would say we're waiting too long. She's probably right, but I'd rather be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An electrician's apprenticeship at Samir's age: realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Samir is twenty-nine, not ninety, and a trade is more realistic than waiting for the bakery to save him. His cousin Faisal took on a thirty-year-old last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like real time. I could have a family by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. Employers and families can sort this out without a big government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be all right, if we planned. I'd have children in the next few years, then train as a nursing associate in my early thirties. The robots wouldn't come for hands-on care until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd carry on at Kindly Hands and save harder for the house. We'd try for a baby next year, as we'd planned. Samir would start looking at trades with his cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still money worries, but not dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything with AI in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more than now, maybe, as others pick it up. For letters and forms. I'd not let it plan my family, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do something with your hands and your heart, and always have a trade to fall back on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Samir and I would both lose our work just when we're trying to start a family. What would help is apprenticeships you can do while earning, for both of us, and employers being made to train people instead of just letting them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the clients who don't speak much English. If they're given a robot, they'll be even lonelier than they already are. Language is half of care.

portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old carer** in a market town, often matched with clients who speak her language.
She lives with her husband Samir, a bakery van driver, and has **three weeks' savings**.
Her own job feels safe in mild worlds; **Samir's work** is the household's weak point.
With faster AGI, she'd **pause children** and lean on family and faith before government.
She favours **earn-while-you-learn** apprenticeships and tries tools once others have.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing both jobs while starting a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for her and Samir while they earn.
Employers made to **train people** instead of letting them go.
